facts.F1: The defendant was granted a tenancy of the premises by the plaintiff commencing on the 5th of February 1969 for the period of one year at a rental of $500 per month by a tenancy agreement dated the 28th of March 1969.
facts.F2: The defendant held over as a monthly tenant at the rental of $580 per month from the 5th of February 1970.
facts.F3: The defendant and the plaintiff signed another tenancy agreement for the premises for another year commencing on the 1st of July 1970 expiring on the 30th of June 1971, at the monthly rental of $700 per month on the 28th of July 1970.
facts.F4: The second tenancy agreement was sent by both of the parties, to the Secretariat of Home Affairs for ratification and which was duly ratified on the 29th of July 1970.
facts.F5: The defendant and the plaintiff entered into another tenancy agreement on the 17th of July 1971 for another year for the premises commencing on the 1st of July 1971 expiring on the 30th of June 1972.
facts.F6: The 1971 tenancy agreement was also forwarded by the party to the Secretariat for Home Affairs for ratification pursuant to Section 5(1) of the tenancy (Notice of Termination) Ordinance 1962 Cap.335 and was duly ratified.
facts.F7: There is no option granted in the third tenancy agreement dated the 17th of July 1971.
facts.F8: The plaintiff wrote to the defendant stating that the tenancy agreement would expire on the 30th of June 1972 and that the defendant was requested to deliver vacant possession of the premises on the 30th of June to the plaintiff on the 3rd of June 1972.
facts.F9: The defendant replied that the plaintiff had no right to give notice because she was a protected tenant of the premises under Rent Increases (Domestic Premises Control) Ordinance 1970.
facts.F10: The defendant alleged that she was under the impression that if she did not execute the 1970 tenancy agreement she would not be allowed to exercise her option to renew the tenancy agreement in respect of the other adjoining premises.
facts.F11: The defendant alleged that the contents of the 1970 tenancy agreement were in English and never explained to her fully.
facts.F12: The defendant notionally rendered vacant possession and surrendered her monthly tenancy existing in June 1970 by executing the tenancy agreements in 1970 and 1971.
facts.F13: The defendant is estopped from denying that there had been any new tenancy since July 1970 by her own conduct.
facts.F14: The new tenancy has now expired by effluxion of time without any option for renewal.

reference_issues: Whether the defendant surrendered her monthly tenancy existing in June 1970 by executing further tenancy agreement in 1970 and 1971.

facts.F2: The plaintiff got off the MTR train at Wong Tai Sin Station and was ascending the staircase at Exit A.
facts.F3: He saw four election promoters of the Third Party standing on the landing at the top of the staircase, blocking the better half of the exit.
facts.F4: When the plaintiff was about four to five steps below the promoters, he began to veer right.
facts.F5: When the plaintiff was about one to two steps from them, the promoter on his left suddenly waved the placard haphazardly and hit his left eye.

claim: application for new tenancy and determination of prevailing market rent
requested_remedy: application for new tenancy and determination of prevailing market rent

facts.F1: The applicant (John James Toohey) and respondent (Hero Plaza Limited) entered into a renewed tenancy agreement for the subject premises (Flat C, 15 Tung Shan Terrace, Hong Kong) for a term of 2 years from 1 May 1996 to 30 April 1998.
facts.F2: In December 1999, the respondent served a Form CR101 to terminate the tenancy on 30 June 1999, which the applicant responded to with a Form CR102 in February 2000.
facts.F3: The parties resolved their dispute over the validity of the applicant's Form CR102 and consented that the applicant should be entitled to a new tenancy commencing from 1 July 1999.
facts.F4: The subject premises was renovated in 1999, and the experts for both parties agreed on the saleable area (76.7 sq.m.) and the area of the terrace (68.3 sq.m.).
facts.F5: The expert surveyor for the applicant, Mr. Simon Lynch, reported defects in the premises, including water pipes furring, low hot water pressure, and poor electricity supply.
facts.F6: Mr. Lynch used the direct comparison method of valuation and analyzed six comparables from the Rating and Valuation Department, ultimately adopting a unit rental value of $230 per sq.m.
facts.F7: The respondent's expert, Mr. Rock Tsang, adopted a single comparable (23 Tung Shan Terrace, 2/F, Flat A) and made adjustments for various factors, resulting in a unit rate of $263.82 per sq.m.
facts.F8: The tribunal rejected Mr. Tsang's methodology and considered other Tung Shan Terrace comparables in determining the prevailing market rent.
facts.F9: The tribunal considered multiple Tung Shan Terrace comparables and determined the average rate of $244.45 per sq.m. from the four 23 Tung Shan Terrace comparables.
facts.F10: The tribunal took into account view and level adjustments in determining the prevailing market rent.

reference_issues: Determination of the prevailing market rent for the subject premises commencing from 1 July 1999

claim: declaration that the requisitions numbered 4, 5 and 6 in the letter dated 18 January 1999 from the Purchaser's solicitors to FWH had not been satisfactorily answered by the Defendant; entitlement to terminate the Agreement; repayment of the deposit and the amount of stamp duty paid by the Plaintiff, interest and costs
requested_remedy: declaration that the requisitions numbered 4, 5 and 6 in the letter dated 18 January 1999 from the Purchaser's solicitors to FWH had not been satisfactorily answered by the Defendant; entitlement to terminate the Agreement; repayment of the deposit and the amount of stamp duty paid by the Plaintiff, interest and costs

facts.F1: A provisional agreement for sale and purchase was entered into between the parties on 9 December 1998, with the subject of the sale and purchase being Unit E, 24/F, Block 1, Richland Gardens, No. 80 Wang Kwong Road, Kowloon, Hong Kong.
facts.F2: The consideration was HK$1,660,000.00, with 10% (HK$166,000) paid by the Plaintiff as deposit and part payment on or before the signing of the Agreement.
facts.F3: Completion of the sale and purchase was to take place on or before 9 February 1999, with time being of the essence of the Agreement.
facts.F4: The Purchaser's solicitors noticed from the land search records that the Property was subject to two encumbrances: a writ of summons issued on 17 May 1991 in High Court Action No. A3642 of 1991, and a sealed copy order in the High Court Action dated 22 March 1993.
facts.F5: The High Court Order declared that Mr. Cheung was entitled to 45% of the beneficial interest in the Property, subject to the approval of the Housing Authority and/or any other competent authority.
facts.F6: The Purchaser's solicitors raised requisitions about the High Court Order, including the need for Mr. Cheung to release or assign his beneficial interest in the Property to the Defendant.
facts.F7: The Purchaser's solicitors received a sealed copy of the Family Court Order, which required Mr. Cheung to transfer his 45% beneficial interest in the Property to the Defendant.
facts.F8: The Purchaser's solicitors raised further requisitions, including the need for an assignment by Mr. Cheung of his interest in the Property to the Defendant.
facts.F9: FWH, the Defendant's solicitors, asserted that Mr. Cheung had no further interest in the Property and that no assignment was necessary, but this was deemed unsatisfactory by the court.
facts.F10: The Purchaser's solicitors proposed to FWH to extend the completion date to 21 April 1999, but FWH did not respond.
facts.F11: Y&A, the Defendant's new solicitors, suggested that the Defendant apply to the Family Court for an order to the effect that when Mr. Cheung transferred his interest to the Defendant, there would be no necessity to execute any assignment or related document.
facts.F12: The Purchaser's solicitors replied that an assignment by Mr. Cheung was necessary and that good title to the Property had not been shown.
facts.F13: The Purchaser's solicitors terminated the Agreement and demanded the return of the deposits.
facts.F14: The Defendant subsequently registered a memorandum of determination of the Agreement in the Land Registry in September 1999 and sold the Property to another purchaser in November that year at a lower price.
facts.F15: The court found that the High Court Order did not declare that Mr. Cheung's interest was vested in the Defendant.
facts.F16: The Purchaser's solicitors had raised valid points about the Family Court Order and the requisitions were matters which may be reasonably and fairly questioned by competent persons.
facts.F17: The court applied the principle that a good title is one which can at all times and in all circumstances be forced upon an unwilling purchaser in an action for specific performance, and that the court will not force a doubtful title on a purchaser.
facts.F18: Requisitions numbered 4, 5, and 6 referred to the need for Mr. Cheung to assign his interest in the Property to the Defendant

reference_issues: Whether the Defendant had shown good title to the Property and answered the requisitions satisfactorily
Whether the Plaintiff was entitled to terminate the Agreement and claim repayment of the deposit and stamp duty

parties: Plaintiff: THE JOINT AND SEVERAL TRUSTEES OF THE PROPERTY OF YIP YAM YU ALEX

facts.F1: The 1st Respondent (YIP YAM YU ALEX) is a bankrupt and the 2nd Respondent (KO SUK CHING) is his Mother.
facts.F2: They are the registered tenants in common of the subject residential property at Flat C, 35/F, Tower 16, Caribbean Coast, Crystal Cove, Tung Chung.
facts.F3: The Mother sold her restaurant business in the United Kingdom after living abroad with the Son for about 15 years.
facts.F4: The Mother had a considerable sum of savings resulting from operation of the restaurant and the proceeds of sale of the business.
facts.F5: The Son and the Mother moved back to Hong Kong in about 2005 and decided to settle in Hong Kong by 2007.
facts.F6: They lived in rented accommodation until they bought the Property.
facts.F7: The Mother purchased Flat A on the same floor of the Property in her sole name for HK$3,390,000.
facts.F8: The Son and the Mother purchased the uncompleted Property for HK$2,090,000 as joint tenants.
facts.F9: The Son executed a mortgage deed (the BEA Mortgage) in respect of the Property with the Bank of East Asia Limited.
facts.F10: The BEA Mortgage was to secure two loans granted to the Son and the Mother as joint borrowers.
facts.F11: The loans were fully repaid in 2 years on 4 November 2009 by transferring two sums of HK$299,474.24 and HK$475,228.81 from the Mother's bank account to the joint account maintained by the Mother and the Son.
facts.F12: The Son issued a Notice of Severance to sever the joint tenancy on 31 October 2013 and the Property has been held by the Son and the Mother as tenants in common in equal shares since then.

parties: Plaintiff: Doo Yuen Sun Wilber Sonny

facts.F1: The Applicant is the tenant, and the Respondent is the landlord of the subject premises known as 2nd Floor, Penthouse and one Car Parking Space, 34G Braga Circuit.
facts.F2: The Premises was subject to a monthly tenancy at a rental of $20,000 per month, on inclusive of rates basis.
facts.F3: The Applicant has been occupying the Premises for more than 20 years without a written tenancy agreement.
facts.F4: The parties agreed that the Tribunal should grant a new tenancy of the Premises for a term of 2 years commencing from 1 August 2003, on the same terms as before.
facts.F5: The Respondent estimated the monthly rent at $17,700, whilst the Applicant estimated it at $22,500, both on the basis of exclusive of rates and management fee but inclusive of one car parking space.
facts.F6: The Rating & Valuation Department's assessment was not considered relevant to the choice of comparables.
facts.F7: Comparable 7 had a unique location and high noise level that made it unsuitable for comparison.
facts.F8: The Premises had yard/extension, open roof, and a penthouse.
facts.F9: The car parking space was included in the tenancy.
facts.F10: Construction disturbance, size, lease type, and provision of domestic appliance were factors considered for adjustment.
facts.F11: No adjustment was made for view/aspect and water penetration.

claim: The plaintiff alleges that the defendants occupied a piece of land and a mooring at Marina Cove by trespass.

facts.F2: The plaintiff alleges that the third defendant wrongfully demolished a wall partitioning the garden, and then wrongfully entered and took possession of the garden forming part of E3 and the adjoining mooring.
facts.F3: The defendants claim that the plaintiff sold the piece of land, including a garden, to the third defendant with an exclusive right to occupy the mooring.
facts.F4: The defendants claim that the plaintiff misrepresented the boundary of the garden and the exclusive right to use the mooring.

facts.F7: The defendants claim that the written agreement and assignment should be rectified to reflect the oral agreement.
facts.F8: Mr Heung and two independent witnesses, Leung Chat Wai and Ian Nicholas Bebbington, testified in support of Mr Heung's account of the events.
facts.F9: The plaintiff's evidence was inherently unreliable and contradicted by other evidence.
facts.F10: A survey by Mr Henry Chan was conducted and used as the basis for rectifying the written agreement and assignment.

lawsuit_type: Trespass allegation and claim for rectification of commercial contract
reference_issues: Whether the defendants have trespassed on the plaintiff's land by occupying the piece of land in question.
Whether the defendants are entitled to have the written agreement and assignment rectified based on the oral agreement with the plaintiff.

claim: Claim for possession of a flat on the third floor of the Marco Polo Mansion
requested_remedy: Claim for possession of a flat on the third floor of the Marco Polo Mansion
parties: Plaintiff: The plaintiff landlord (not explicitly named in the text)
Defendant: The 2nd defendant (not explicitly named in the text)

facts.F1: The 1st defendant moved into the premises in 1968 under a lease for one year commencing from the 1st January.
facts.F2: The 1st defendant continued to live there with his family until the 14th August 1971 when he purchased for himself another flat in the same building.
facts.F3: The 1st defendant sublet to the 2nd defendant as from the 16th August 1971, but for a term of one year and 4 ½ months.
facts.F4: The plaintiff granted a further lease to the 1st defendant, only on this occasion breaking the earlier practice by making it for a period of two years, at the end of 1971.
facts.F5: The plaintiff was resident in the United States of America and his affairs were managed by his attorney in Hong Kong.
facts.F6: The attorney received information from the plaintiff that he was returning to Hong Kong to get married and would need his flat for himself and his wife to live in.
facts.F7: The attorney broke the news to the 1st defendant asking for the return of the premises as soon as possible in March 1973.
facts.F8: The lease contained a simple clause against subletting and the 1st defendant felt that he was left with no alternative other than to own up to his wrongful conduct.
facts.F9: A writ of possession grounded upon the unlawful subletting was served upon the 1st defendant on the 30th March 1973.
facts.F10: The existence of the sub-lease became known to the plaintiff's attorney sometime in or about July 1972.
facts.F11: The 2nd defendant continued to pay and the 1st defendant continued to receive rent from the 1st January 1972 up to at least the 28th February 1973.
facts.F12: The plaintiff's attorney was well aware of the sub-tenancy and must be taken to have waived any right the plaintiff may have had to re-enter for breach of covenant in this respect.
facts.F13: The grant of the sub-lease by the 1st defendant operated as an assignment until the end of 1971.
facts.F14: The grant of a fresh lease to the 1st defendant as from the 1st of January of the following year took effect, replacing the earlier assignment.
facts.F15: The 2nd defendant was a monthly sub-tenant of the 1st defendant from the 1st January 1972 up to at least the 28th February 1973.

reference_issues: Whether the sub-lease granted by the 1st defendant was an assignment or a sub-lease.
Whether the plaintiff's attorney had knowledge of the sub-lease at the time of granting a new lease to the 1st defendant.
Whether the plaintiff's attorney had waived any right to re-enter for breach of covenant.

facts.F1: The property in question is a free-standing village house situated at Tai Hang Hau, Clearwater Bay.
facts.F2: The house was constructed on Lot 534 Demarcation District 230, which is held by virtue of a lease from the Government subject to certain conditions contained in building licence no. 1007 dated 22 December 1981.
facts.F3: The licence allows for certain permitted construction and use, and provides that any portion of the lot not built upon must be used for agricultural or garden purposes.
facts.F4: The licence also includes a clause giving the Crown (now the Government) the right of re-entry without compensation in the event of default.
facts.F5: The plaintiff is an indigenous villager and the original owner of the vacant lot, which was given to him by his father.
facts.F6: The plaintiff built a house on the lot and was later told by the District Lands Officer that it conformed to licence 1007.
facts.F7: The plaintiff subsequently built a swimming pool on the grounds without approval from the Building Authority or District Lands Officer.
facts.F8: In March 1997, the plaintiff listed the property for sale, which led to a provisional agreement being entered into with the defendant, represented by Ng King Ming.
facts.F9: The parties engaged solicitors and a formal agreement was signed on 22 April 1997, with the purchase price set at $11 million.
facts.F10: The agreement stated that time was of the essence, and that the vendor must assign the property to the purchaser free from all incumbrances.
facts.F11: The agreement also included a clause that the purchaser was deemed to have inspected and made all necessary enquiries, and was satisfied with the existing state, condition, and finishes of the property.
facts.F12: Completion was originally due on 15 December 1997, but was deferred until 25 February 1998, with an additional deposit of $1.1 million and $100,000.00 in compensation for the delay.
facts.F13: The defendant's application for mortgage assistance was successful, but was subject to a favourable surveyor's report.
facts.F14: A surveyor's report raised concerns about the legality of the swimming pool, leading to a dispute between the parties.
facts.F15: The defendant's solicitors, CLW, claimed that the plaintiff was in breach of the agreement, while the plaintiff's solicitors, C W Heung, argued that any objection to title was out of time.

Whether the defendant waived its rights to object to the plaintiff's title by its conduct

claim: The Applicant sought a declaratory order that the 1994 increase and/or the 1995 increase were void ab initio and of no effect. They were in breach of the mandatory provisions implied into the DMC by Section 34E of the Building Management Ordinance, Cap.344 (BMO), and Paragraph 1 of the Seventh Schedule of the same Ordinance. They were also inconsistent with the provisions of Clause D3 of Section V of the DMC. The Applicant also asked for a declaratory order for the proper calculation, apportionment and determination of the monthly management fees payable by the Applicant for the Ground floor and Third floor.
requested_remedy: The Applicant sought a declaratory order that the 1994 increase and/or the 1995 increase were void ab initio and of no effect. They were in breach of the mandatory provisions implied into the DMC by Section 34E of the Building Management Ordinance, Cap.344 (BMO), and Paragraph 1 of the Seventh Schedule of the same Ordinance. They were also inconsistent with the provisions of Clause D3 of Section V of the DMC. The Applicant also asked for a declaratory order for the proper calculation, apportionment and determination of the monthly management fees payable by the Applicant for the Ground floor and Third floor.

facts.F1: The Applicant has been the owner of the Ground floor and Third floor of the Watson Building since 10th May 1985.
facts.F2: The first Respondent (R1) was the registered owner of the whole of the Building until 17th March 1982, when it assigned the 13th floor of the Building to a second owner.
facts.F3: A Deed of Mutual Covenant (DMC) was executed and registered in the Tsuen Wan New Territories Land Registry under Memorial Number 248727 and later re-registered under Memorial Number 267737.
facts.F4: Under the DMC, R1 was appointed to be the first manager of the Building for a term of seven years from 17th March 1982, and thereafter until the termination of the appointment.
facts.F5: There are a total of 402,475 undivided shares in the building, with the Ground floor allotted 75,000 shares and the Third floor allotted 30,631 shares.
facts.F6: There is no incorporation of owners, nor is there an owners’ committee.
facts.F7: The second Respondent (R2) took over the management of the Building, although there was no formal documentary evidence to that effect.
facts.F8: The Applicant accepts that R2 is the de facto manager.
facts.F9: R1 and R2 have common directors and shareholders.
facts.F10: On 27th March 1997, R1 sold off all its remaining interest in the Building to Grace Magic Limited.
facts.F11: The Applicant was under the impression that previous increases in management fees were on account of inflation.
facts.F12: On 1st October 1994, the monthly management fees for the Ground floor were increased to $6,000 from $4,922.28, and that for the Third floor was increased to $11,400 from $9,424.88 (the 1994 increase).
facts.F13: On 1st December 1995, the management fees for the Ground floor were increased to $37,500 per month, and that for the Third floor was increased to $15,315.50 (the 1995 increase).
facts.F14: The Applicant protested against the 1995 increase by a letter dated 18th December 1995 addressed to R2.
facts.F15: The Applicant demanded to see the accounts relating to the Building’s expenses, and statements of income and expenditure, under Section V Section H of the DMC.
facts.F16: None of the procedures required under the BMO for increase of management fees had been followed.
facts.F17: The Respondents produced certain accounts, including audited financial statements, bank statements, and management fee receipts.
facts.F18: The auditors’ report stated that a proper system of internal accounting control had not been in place for the periods in question.
facts.F19: The 1993 rate was set as the baseline for payment of management fees until the proper determination of the fees under the provisions of the Seventh Schedule of the Building Management Ordinance.

reference_issues: Whether the 1994 and 1995 increases in management fees were valid and in accordance with the BMO and the DMC.
Whether the Applicant had acquiesced or waived its rights in relation to the increases in management fees.
Whether the Respondents had complied with the procedures required under the BMO for increase of management fees.

claim: The plaintiff seeks to recover possession of various post-war premises in a building located at 108-110 Castle Peak Road, Kowloon, due to a plan to redevelop the site.

facts.F1: The building at 108-110 Castle Peak Road, Kowloon, was built in 1949 and had been poorly maintained, resulting in its dilapidated state.
facts.F2: Avion Investment Ltd (the landlord) seeks to redevelop the site into a 15-story building containing 24 domestic units and 10 commercial units.
facts.F3: The proposed new building would be larger and have a gross floor area of 1483 square meters compared to the current 715 square meters.
facts.F4: The landlord has obtained approval from the Building Authority for the redevelopment plan.
facts.F5: However, the redevelopment plan faces a problem due to an informal transaction that took place in 1984 between the then-landlord and Mr. Lee Tung Chau (Mr. Lee), who is a respondent.
facts.F6: The transaction was verbal, did not involve a written assignment, and involved the transfer of Mr. Lee Chik Fook's tenancy to Mr. Lee, without any formal documentation or surrender of vacant possession of the premises.
facts.F7: There is uncertainty over whether Mr. Lee's tenancy is governed by Part II or Part IV of the Landlord and Tenant (Consolidation) Ordinance (Cap. 7).
facts.F8: If Mr. Lee's tenancy was not properly assigned, then the current sub-tenants may have automatically become direct tenants of the landlord under section 119P(8) of Cap. 7.
facts.F9: The Tribunal is restricted in awarding costs due to sections 68 and 119R of Cap. 7.
facts.F10: The landlord was unable to prove that it has the financial ability to carry out the proposed redevelopment.
facts.F11: The landlord failed to meet the requirements of sections 53A(1) and 119F(1) of the Landlord and Tenant (Consolidation) Ordinance (Cap. 7).
facts.F12: There is uncertainty over when the rebuilding work should be commenced or completed due to uncertainty over Mr. Lee's tenancy and the current sub-tenants' status.
facts.F13: The Tribunal cannot estimate the landlord's future prospects of recovering possession of the premises on the 3rd floor of 108 Castle Peak Road.

reference_issues: Whether Mr. Lee's tenancy was validly assigned to Mr. Lee
Whether the Tribunal has the power to award costs in this matter
Whether the landlord should be granted possession of the premises
Whether the landlord has complied with the mandatory conditions for redevelopment under the Landlord and Tenant (Consolidation) Ordinance (Cap. 7)

requested_remedy: claims to be entitled to a ¼ undivided share in the relevant land

facts.F1: The plaintiff claims to be entitled to a ¼ undivided share in the land, which is the remaining portion of Section B of Lot No.636 in Demarcation District No. 124, Ping Shan, Yuen Long in the New Territories.
facts.F2: The second defendant denies that the plaintiff has a relevant interest in the land.
facts.F3: In 1903, three pieces of paddy fields, including the one in question, were sold by the Min Sun Tso family to Yick Ting.
facts.F4: In 1906, the land was described in a Block Crown Lease as having an area of 15.08 acres and being owned by Tang Sze I Tong.
facts.F5: In 1920, the property was divided, with the tong and its family elders employing proper machinery, including a public notice and a memorial, to have the division recorded.
facts.F6: The plaintiff's claim is through Tang Pak Yun, who was a party to the 1920 division.
facts.F7: The defendants also claim interests in the land under the 1920 division.
facts.F8: In 1943, an instrument was executed which attempted to give Tang Pak Yun a specific quarter of the field.
facts.F9: The British administration recognized Chinese custom and customary rights, including the ability to hold land and deal with it as any natural person could.
facts.F10: The tong's ownership of the property was dealt with in the 1920 division through proper machinery, including a public notice and a memorial.
facts.F11: Tang Pak Yun was intended to become the owner of a ¼ undivided share, which is consistent with evidence as to the way in which the produce of the land was dealt with and the way in which the Crown rent was paid.

claim: The plaintiffs claim that the defendant has wrongfully erected a building on Lot 3590 which encroaches upon their land, Lot 3443, and seek an injunction restraining the defendant from continuing the trespass and encroachment, an order for vacant possession of Lot 3443, damages for trespass of Lot 3443, and costs.
requested_remedy: The plaintiffs claim that the defendant has wrongfully erected a building on Lot 3590 which encroaches upon their land, Lot 3443, and seek an injunction restraining the defendant from continuing the trespass and encroachment, an order for vacant possession of Lot 3443, damages for trespass of Lot 3443, and costs.
parties: Plaintiff: Kam Kan Cho (, Kan Pak Kin ()

facts.F1: The plaintiffs are the registered owners of a piece of land situate in Tai Tau Ling Village in Sheung Shui in the New Territories, Lot 3443.
facts.F2: The defendant is the registered owner of the land directly adjacent to the plaintiffs' land, Lot 3590.
facts.F3: The plaintiffs' father purchased Lot 3443 in May 1958.
facts.F4: A house had been erected on Lot 22, adjacent to Lot 3443, prior to the DD survey in 1898.
facts.F5: The plaintiffs' father built a single-storey house on Lot 3443 in 1958, using the western wall of the defendant's house on Lot 3590 and the eastern wall of the house on Lot 22 as walls.
facts.F6: In 1982-83, the house on Lot 22 was redeveloped, and the defendant demolished the old house on Lot 3590 and rebuilt.
facts.F7: The defendant's new house on Lot 3590 encroaches upon Lot 3443 by 0.554 metres on the northern boundary and 0.638 metres on the southern boundary.
facts.F8: Aerial photographs taken in 1964, 1972, 1981, 1982, and 1983 show the development of the area, including the demolition and reconstruction of the houses on Lot 22 and Lot 3590.
facts.F9: Expert evidence from Dr. Bruce King and Mr. Thomas Lee was presented on the interpretation of aerial photographs and the measurement of dimensions.
facts.F10: The plaintiffs' mother specifically objected to any encroachment in the course of the reconstruction.
facts.F11: The defendant did not abandon possession of the land before the full period of adverse possession had run.

The date at which the encroachment first occurred.
The effect of the Extension Ordinance on the defendant's rights under the Limitation Ordinance.
Whether there was a gap in the adverse possession between the time at which the first house on Lot 3590 was demolished and the new house was constructed.
Whether the defendant is entitled to a declaration of proprietary estoppel.

claim: declaration that the contents of the Notice of Third Party Interest registered against the said premises are false and therefore null and void and exemplary damages against the Defendant
requested_remedy: declaration that the contents of the Notice of Third Party Interest registered against the said premises are false and therefore null and void and exemplary damages against the Defendant

facts.F1: The Plaintiff and the Defendant were husband and wife and got married on the 31st of October 1981.
facts.F2: A decree nisi was made on the 23rd of October 1992 which decree was made absolute on the 16th of December 1992.
facts.F3: The decree was granted towards a petition by the Defendant for a divorce on the ground of a two years separation with consent.
facts.F4: In a separation agreement dated July 1989, the parties agreed that each party shall not be liable to the other, nor interfere with each other, and shall not go for his/her own futures.
facts.F5: By a deed of assignment dated 21st of December 1987, the Plaintiff became the registered owner of the premises at Unit B, Ground Floor, No. 13 Yung Shui Long New Village, Lamma Island.
facts.F6: The Defendant registered a Notice of Third Party Interest against the said premises, claiming that he paid the entire purchase price and was the true and sole beneficial owner of the premises.
facts.F7: The Plaintiff and the Defendant purchased a premises at Flat No. 11 on the 12th Floor, Moon Wah Building, Nos. 9-23 Sui Man Road, Hong Kong in March 1981.
facts.F8: The purchase price was financed by contributions from the Plaintiff, the Defendant, his brother-in-law, and his mother.
facts.F9: The Defendant was investigated by the ICAC in July 1985 and assigned his share of the Moon Wah premises to the Plaintiff by a Deed of Gift.
facts.F10: The Defendant was convicted of bribery offenses and sentenced to 18 months imprisonment.
facts.F11: The Moon Wah premises was sold for $250,000.00 and a sum of $250,000.00 was paid into the Plaintiff's account.
facts.F12: The Plaintiff transferred $140,000.00 into the Defendant's account on the 28th of December 1987.
facts.F13: The Defendant claimed that the sum of $140,000.00 was not his share of the proceeds of the sale of the Moon Wah premises but was from a profit of about $300,000.00 in cash accumulated from trading in furs in Japan.
facts.F14: The Defendant suggested that he had been trading in furs in Japan and at the material time, a profit of about $300,000.00 in cash had been accumulated and was put in a cash deposit box in the name of the Plaintiff.
facts.F15: The Plaintiff denied the Defendant's allegation and claimed that the purchase price of the said premises was entirely funded by herself.
facts.F16: The trading in furs was a joint effort on the part of both the Plaintiff and the Defendant.
facts.F17: The Defendant had never claimed to be entitled to the said property before he registered the Notice of Third Party Interest.
facts.F18: The Notice of Third Party Interest was registered without the Plaintiff knowing about it.

reference_issues: Who funded the purchase of the said premises?

If the Defendant contributed wholly or in part to the purchase price, whether the doctrine of presumption of advancement operates against him and if not, to what extent he should be entitled to the proceeds of the sale of the said premises.
Whether it is a proper case to award exemplary damages against the Defendant.
